Hello,

I am encountering an error message that I do not understand and am looking for anyone who may be able to help figure it out.

I ran a forced choice experiment to test whether speakers of Thai prefer one of two nonce monosyllable stimuli. Stimuli are all CV:, with only tone varying within each pair. Across pairs, I vary vowel quality, onset place and onset manner. In each stimulus pair, one of the stimuli has L tone, with the other being either H or R. As a result I have two levels for tone (H and R). Onset manner has three levels (aspirated, unaspirated, voiced). Onset place has 4 levels (alveolar, bilabial, palatal, velar). Vowel quality has 9 levels (a, E, i, ia, o, O, u, U, ua, Ua). I computed lexical neighborhood density (LND) and Orthographic Cumulative Biphone Probability (OCBP) based on corpus statistics and so these are numerical, continuous variables. Reponses are coded as 0 if the L tone stimulus was chosen and as 1 if an H or R tone stimulus was chosen.

I am using a linear mixed model with the 4 categorical and 2 continuous fixed effects and a random effect ("participant") (there were 14 participants). messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeremy,
 
The message itself actually has little or nothing to do with the cause of the error. I'm surprised there isn't a specific message for this problem.
 
pvals.fnc() function isn't implemented for generalized linear mixed models (including the logistic regression you're using by setting the family as binomial). You don't really need to use it anyway as, when you build a generalized linear mixed model using the lme4 package, the p values are calculated for you using the Wald test. The p values are in the final column of the fixed effects section of the model summary -- there's a significant effect of tone.
 
HTH,
 
Ian

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeremy,
 
I've also read that the Wald test is conservative, although I was under the impression that this was only when the sample size is small. As is often the case in these matters nobody ever defines "small", but your 1500+ observations doesn't seem too small* I guess if you were really concerned that you were missing effects because the Wald test lacked power then you could either collect more data or implement your models using a different package. Of course, you should do that after taking steps to reduce the possibility of multicollinearity (e.g. centering your predictors).
 
I don't know of anything for R that will give you MCMC simulations for logistic mixed effects, but there's no doubt software out there somewhere that does it -- a cursory glance at Google suggests MLwIN might -- and since you don't have to worry about crossed random effects you shouldn't be too restricted in your options.
 
*although, as more of a sidenote, with less than 1600 observations I'd be reluctant to put much faith in the results of a regression with 18 fixed effects, but not sure that MCMC would be any less vulnerable to that problem than Wald. It might be worth asking whether, for example, a difference in preference between the vowels "a" and "i" has some relevance for the theory you're trying to test, or whether you might be better of by dealing with some of your fixed effects in different ways e.g. as random effects.
 
HTH,
 
Ian

messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

I conducted multiple (>12) forced-choice experiments with three possible
categorical responses, and two categorical predictors each with two levels.
Two of the responses are what I'm interested in, but the third was actually
a distractor category that fit very clearly with half of the filler items.
 Most participants never categorize a target item with this distractor
response, but a very small number do (0-2 individuals per experiment will
use the distractor variable for 1-5 responses. For some experiments it is
never chosen with target items. It's clearly associated with certain
individuals, and seems to indicate people who aren't taking the experiment
seriously, or are unable to do the task. Actually, I reran the experiment
for any participants that used the distractor category for more than two
responses, and replaced them. Now I'm wondering if I can actually do this.)

I am not interested in these distractor responses. My question is:

1) Can I simply ignore these responses, remove them and treat my dataset as
if there were only two categories? This means I will sometimes have fewer
responses for some individuals, but I can run a regular lmer, which seems
infinitely easier than the alternative.

2) If I retain the distractor responses, do I have to resort to
multinominal logistic regression? I've looked at
http://hlplab.wordpress.com/2009/05/07/multinomial-random-effects-models-in-r/,
the tutorial and http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/r/dae/mlogit.htm, but it
seems complex, difficult to interpret, not clear to me what I would then
report, and frankly overkill for the simple advantage of including a
response level that I am sure is irrelevant.

Perhaps someone can suggest a simple principled way to show that the
distractor variable has a minimal effect?
Or maybe there is some new alternative to MCMCglmm? (I see the tutorial and
the hlplab post are all from 2009...)

Thanks for any help,

/Jennifer

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jennifer,
 
Without knowing what the "responses-of-interest" are and how they differ from the distractor it's hard to say for sure, but if generally the only people choosing them are "bad" participants (and you may want to have a sound reason for why you're more likely to choose them if you're not interested or not able) then it seems reasonable to use them as an exclusion criteria. Much in the same way as, if you were using an online measure (eye-tracking, EEG etc.), you might have participants answer comprehension questions and exclude anybody who scored under, say, 75%.
 
You could either exclude any participant who chose a distractor or, less strictly, exclude those who chose them over a certain percentage of trials and for those who only occassionally chose them (below your criteria) just exclude that trial. You might want to check whether the distractor responses are more common in a particular condition: count the distractor responses per cell and then use a Chi-Square test.
 
I don't know a huge amount about multinomial regression (mixed effects or not) but it sounds like the distractor responses are pretty infrequent, and you're always on shaky ground when you try and model rare outcomes.
 
Ian

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm trying to model the contribution of corpus frequency ("FreqGerman") 
to the probability with which participants are able to translate a word 
into their L1 ("Correct", a binary factor).

Word frequency was highly skewed, so I log-transformed it: 
log.FreqGerman = log(FreqGerman + 1). (I added 1 to each word frequency 
in order to avoid transformed values of -Inf for word frequencies of 0.)

It seems that the effect of the log-transformed frequency measure on 
translation accuracy is itself non-linear, too. I've added the visual 
output of a logistic GAM model with log.FreqGerman as a non-linear 
predictor and random intercepts for participants and item as an attachment.

A host of other variables enter into the model that I'm trying to 
construct, and all of them (except for log.FreqGerman) are well 
approximated by linear terms. I therefore would prefer to model my data 
using a GLMM, whilst doing justice to the non-linear frequency effect. 
It seems that there are substantial interindividual differences in the 
sensitivity to word frequency, which I could model in a GLMM, but I'm 
unsure how to do this in a GAM with mixed effects.

How should I best proceed?

I've tried the following:

1) Carry out an additional logarithmic transformation: loglog.FreqGerman 
= log(log(FreqGerman+1)+1). Compute GLMM incl. random slope for this 
variable:

model = lmer(Correct ~ var1 + var2 + ... + cloglog.FreqGerman +
                         (1+cloglog.FreqGerman|Subject) +
                         (1+var1+var2|Stimulus),
                       data = dat, family=binomial)

Using cloglog.FreqGerman gives an appreciably lower AIC value than using 
clog.FreqGerman here. (c = centred at the sample mean)

2) Use rcs from the rms package. But can I enter the rcs term as a 
by-subject random slope? That would result in completely different 
by-participant frequency curves, wouldn't it, and the random slopes 
would be quite uninterpretable, right?

Additionally, I thought about fiddling about with some other 
transformations that (unlike the log-log-transformation) result in an 
symptote, e.g. atanlog.FreqGerman = atan(log(FreqGerman+1)+k) (where k 
is some constant), but I'm not sure whether that would be okay and 
whether the random slopes would still be interpretable.

Thanks for your input,

Jan Vanhove

messages.body_plain:
hi Jan,

Just my two cents:
- log-log transforming seems fine to me (though I don't follow why you
need that second +1). The lower AIC could be used to justify it.  It
does strain the ease of interpretation a bit, but it's still monotone
(as freq goes up, the effect does, too), and that's mostly what people
care about, right?
- That said, I think I'd be more worried about over-fitting, meaning
that the more complex curve may not be the best thing.  The reason I
say that is that your plot makes it look like the effect is very close
to linear until somewhere between 5 and 6 log-freq, and then from
there it flattens out and the std errs get huge because there appear
to be very few data points out there above 5.6 or so.  So I think you
should at least consider the possible merits of an approach where you
did something with those extremely-high-frequency items, and just fit
a (generalized) linear model.  To put it another way, it may be that
only a few extreme data points make it look like it's worth doing a
more complex non-linear model, but it might be just as well to
truncate/transform/remove those extreme data points and stick to a
simpler model. Log-log transforming the entire data set may be
overkill if it's just a few points driving the apparent nonlinearity,
but if it improves some extreme outlier fit, it can give the
(misleading) appearance of being a better model.
- you may want to try running GAMs separately for individuals (or
subsets, if you have a lot of people), and maybe plot all the
resulting curves, in order to get an approximate view of how much the
shape of the curve is varying by person. A hierarchical model is a
better analysis tool than separating each person out, because of the
partial pooling across people, but plotting separate GAMs might give
you some insights into what you might be trying to capture in a
hierarchical model.

hope that helps,
-scott

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jan,
Scott makes good points that the pattern looks quite linear except for just
a few observations in the very-high frequency range and that adding
non-linear terms might be over-fitting the data.

That said, if you're very interested in the non-linearity, another option
would be to use a quadratic function, which can be used in a hierarchical
framework and capture individual differences. This is what we do with
fixation time course data and I've used it with word-learning curves that
had approximately the same shape as your data and it seemed to work fairly
well. One downside is that a quadratic is not asymptotic, but that
shouldn't be a problem as long as you're not trying to predict what would
happen at log-Frequencies of 10.

Dan

Hi Iva,

On Mar 29, 2013, at 1:38 PM, Iva Ivanova <iva.m.ivanova-Re5JQEeQqe8AvxtiuMwx3w at public.gmane.org> wrote:

> I have a bunch of structural priming data (in fact, the same ones I had questions about earlier this year). I just realized that I am getting different results depending on the ordering of the factors! I know this is not supposed to happen - any idea where the problem might be?

Yes, that can happen.  The fitting algorithm that estimates your parameters has to assign some portions of the overall variance to each variable (or the error term), and when your predictors are partially collinear, this assignment can go either way.  [There is more "statistics-speak" terminology for this, but I am expressing it in a somewhat intuitive way here.]

If you look at the correlation matrix, you can see that A and B are somewhat collinear (and you're seeing parameter estimates that are somewhat different between the two models).  The interaction is what you presumably care about.  The difference is not huge, but it may be "make or break" for you, given the arbitrarily chosen 0.05 threshold for your p value.

To get around this, center your data.  My favorite centering function can be found on the Jaeger lab's blog.  There is also a good presentation on getting rid of collinearity.  If centering does not help, you have to regress the effect of one predictor  out of the other.  The presentation explains this.  Keep in mind that in this case, you're making the same choice that the fitting algorithm does.  But at least you know your hypothesis and the theory behind it.

http://www.hlp.rochester.edu/resources/WOMM/JaegerKuperman.pdf

Hope that explains it.

Best,
David

Elaborating on what Steve's bringing up: first, we should draw a distinction between the properties of the model that one has specified and the properties of the particular fitting algorithm used when applied to that model (plus a dataset).  Ideally, the fitting algorithm would converge on the truly "best" (maximum likelihood) parameter estimate for the specified model as applied to one's dataset.  In practice, of course, the fitting algorithm only finds an "approximately" best fit, and there is some discrepancy between the fitted model (=the estimate of the model's parameters) that R gives you and what would truly be the *best* parameter estimate for the dataset.  In statistical data analysis you want to be in the situation that the discrepancy is so small that the precise details of the 
 fitting procedure don't matter, and you can abstract away from the fact that the model fit is an approximation and treat it as if it is the *true* best parameter estimate.  In this situation you can focus your attention on model *class* (what set of relationships a particular model definition can specify between one's predictors and predicted values of the response) and interpretation of the individual parameters, because those are the *only* things that matter.

So, first: changing only the order in which the predictors are entered in the R formula changes neither model class nor parameter interpretation.  Thus, Iva, the fact that you found that changing the order in which the predictors are entered affects you results should make you worried: it means that the abstraction I described above (that the details of the fitting algorithm are more or less irrelevant) does not hold.  Between the two models, I would certainly tend to trust the one with singular convergence less than the other, but I would also be concerned about the model fit overall.  (On the other hand, none of the model fits that Iva or Steve reported is dramatically different from any of the others, which is sort of reassuring.)

Second: centering one's predictors does not change model class, and it doesn't change the interpretation of the highest order interaction between the predictors present in your model, either.  (It *does* change the interpretation of the main effects and lower order interactions, which IMHO is generally the only good reason apart, potentially, from model fitting details, to bother centering your predictors: the predictor-centered model might be closer to the parameterization that you really want for interpretive purposes.)  This means that David's advice could potentially be misinterpreted.  I would actually say that if you find that centering your predictors changes results for your highest-order interaction, then it should make you worry about your model fit in general: the abstraction I 
 mentioned above may not be very accurate.

An important proviso about the previous paragraph, which relates to Steve's question, is that this invariance of model class with respect to centering of predictors holds only for certain types of random-effects specifications.  In particular, if you have a random intercept and a random slope for a predictor X but no correlation parameter between the two, the model class is no longer invariant to linear transformations of X (including centering).  We wrote about this in Barr et al 2013 (see footnote 6).

Bottom line for Iva's model interpretation problem: if the question at hand is "is the A:B interaction significant at p<0.05?", I would probably conclude from all this that the interaction between A and B is "likely to be significant-ish" but would be cautious about drawing any firmer conclusions than this from these model fits.  The geekier answer is that I would probably want to cross-check against traditional ANOVA results, and also to play around with convergence tolerance in the lme4 fits to see how sensitive the results are to details of model fitting procedure (but unfortunately I don't know if this is possible in the current version of lme4).

One final question I'd like to throw back out to the R-lang community: as I said before, in Iva's situation I see near-zero value in centering her predictors, except for interpretation of the main effects (and here it'd be better to use deviation coding than to center if one wants main effects in the traditional sense -- AND it's not entirely clear what a "main effect" is in a mixed logit model, which is a whole other story).  However, I'm not sure to what extent it may be the case that predictor-centered models tend to be better from the perspective of the fitting process for mixed logit models -- that is, that the estimates are more stable and the abstraction away from the details of the fitting algorithm is more reliable.  I know that reducing (multi-)collinearity can help deal with cas
 es where the original predictors are very close to being perfectly (multi-)collinear, but Iva's presumably nowhere near this situation (it's a balanced design, right?).  Could anyone shed further light on this issue?

Best & I hope this is useful!

Roger
